In response, we propose an adsorption-coupled solar-powered seawater resource separator (ASP) to simultaneously recover fresh water, lithium and uranium, while generating green electricity. Here, by integrating multi-stage latent heat recovery and multi-field coupled effects, the extraction performance of lithium and uranium under 1 sun irradiation increases by up to 10.2 and 11.6 times, respectively, compared with dark conditions. Outdoor experiments demonstrate that ASP delivers a peak power output of 154.7 W, with a daily water collection rate of 19.82 kg m −2 , alongside lithium and uranium extraction capacities of 4.50 mmol m −2 and 2.64 μmol m −2 , respectively. Economic analysis indicates that ASP can maintain an annual net income exceeding US$20 m −2 . Overall, this work presents an integrated strategy for coupling energy generation, water production and resource recovery, offering a promising pathway towards accelerating Sustainable Development Goals. Energy harvesting Solar energy Main Water, energy, and critical resource security have become increasingly intertwined global challenges, as recognized by Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 6 and 7 (refs. 1 , 2 , 3 ). The accelerating trends in global electrification and digitalization are further intensifying these pressures 4 , 5 . Natural seawater is a vast reservoir of critical resources, such as freshwater, lithium and uranium. Efficient and sustainable extraction of these resources could address the above challenges 6 , 7 , 8 . So far, significant advancements have been made in some seawater resource recovery technologies 9 , 10 . Membrane-based and thermal desalination methods, for instance, have been successfully implemented in water-stressed regions such as the Middle East, mitigating local freshwater shortages 11 , 12 . In comparison, extracting dissolved valuable minerals (for example, lithium and uranium) remains considerably more challenging than freshwater owing to their ultradilute concentrations and competitive ion interference 13 . Over the past decades, multiple extraction strategies have been explored for uranium and lithium extraction from seawater, including electrochemical, photochemical, membrane-based and adsorption-based approaches 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 . While these approaches demonstrate feasibility under laboratory operation, they are often constrained by relatively high energy consumption or operational costs, non-trivial maintenance demands, limited selectivity in complex ionic matrices, risks of secondary waste generation, and so on 18 , 19 (see Supplementary Table 1 for comparison). Several recent efforts have attempted to adapt these strategies for renewable energy-powered off-grid operation, yet their performance remains limited under realistic ocean conditions 20 , 21 . Consequently, realizing continuous, energy-efficient and multi-resource enrichment from seawater under off-grid conditions remains a critical outstanding challenge. Among these technologies, adsorption is widely regarded as one of the most practically deployable strategies due to its low energy requirement, modular configuration and compatibility with off-grid operation 22 . Nevertheless, conventional adsorption devices often exhibit sluggish mass-transfer kinetics and incomplete utilization of active sites in ultradilute environments 21 . Furthermore, most existing extraction systems are designed for single-resource recovery, hindering the simultaneous extraction of multiple valuable resources from seawater. These limitations highlight the need for new extraction architectures that enable continuous and cost-effective multi-resource harvesting under realistic ocean conditions. In this work, we develop an adsorption-coupled solar-powered seawater resource separator (ASP) that integrates a photovoltaic (PV) panel with functionalized capillary wicks (Fig. 1a ).
